summary: The site can say, with sources, that long-term exposure to traffic-related air pollution is associated with higher death rates from heart disease, lung cancer and all causes (HEI 2022: high or moderate-to-high confidence), with new asthma and with chest infections in young children; per-increment risks are modest (about 4-7% per standard increment) and several intervals touch 1. Taiwanese cohorts (MJ Health) link regional PM2.5 to higher mortality (HR 1.15, high vs low), lung cancer in never-smokers (aHR 1.32 per 10 ug/m3), reduced lung function in under-25s, kidney disease and diabetes. IARC lists outdoor air pollution and diesel exhaust as Group 1, but gasoline exhaust only as Group 2B. California shows lung growth improving as air improved. All Taiwanese results are regional-PM2.5 associations, none is scooter-specific, and nothing measured here shows a pedestrian's long-term harm from a red-light scooter queue. WHO guideline values, Taiwan lung cancer statistics, GBD figures and electrification benefit estimates were not obtained.

findings.verifierNote: I opened the HEI Executive Summary PDF and checked every rating in the Executive Summary Table. All ratings listed by the researcher match. Corrections: (1) 10.1016/j.envint.2022.107262 is the DOI of the Boogaard et al. 2022 Environment International paper, not of HEI Special Report 23 itself; cite the report by URL and the paper by DOI. (2) The panel's exposure-level statement is: findings derived from studies conducted when exposure levels were 'generally higher than present-day levels in high-income countries and comparable to or lower than present-day levels in low-income countries'; the researcher's paraphrase dropped the high-income half. (3) 41 of 353 studies (12%) were in Asia, predominantly China; Europe 163 (46%), North America 130 (37%). Also: IHD events MODERATE; coronary events LOW; stroke events LOW to MODERATE (stroke mortality LOW to MODERATE).
findings.claim: The HEI panel rated confidence in an association between long-term traffic-related air pollution (TRAP) and mortality as high for all-cause, circulatory and ischaemic heart disease deaths and moderate-to-high for lung cancer deaths; also moderate-to-high for asthma onset in children and adults and for acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in children.
findings.value: All-cause HIGH; circulatory HIGH; IHD mortality HIGH; lung cancer mortality MODERATE TO HIGH; respiratory mortality MODERATE; stroke mortality LOW TO MODERATE; COPD mortality LOW; asthma onset children MODERATE TO HIGH; asthma onset adults MODERATE TO HIGH; ALRI children MODERATE TO HIGH; ALRI adults VERY LOW TO LOW; COPD incidence LOW; IHD events MODERATE; stroke events LOW TO MODERATE; coronary events LOW; diabetes MODERATE; term low birth weight MODERATE; small for gestational age MODERATE; preterm birth LOW; term birth weight LOW; asthma ever and active asthma in children MODERATE. 353 studies; literature to July 2019.
findings.citation: Health Effects Institute Panel on the Health Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Traffic-Related Air Pollution. 2022. Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Selected Health Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Traffic-Related Air Pollution. HEI Special Report 23. Boston, MA: HEI. Companion paper: Boogaard H, Patton AP, Atkinson RW, et al. 2022. Environment International 164:107262 (title per Crossref: 'Long-term exposure to traffic-related air pollution and selected health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis').
findings.quote: The overall confidence in the evidence for an association between TRAP exposure and mortality was high for all-cause, circulatory, and IHD mortality. The Panel's overall confidence was moderate to high for lung cancer, moderate for respiratory, low to moderate for stroke, and low for COPD mortality.
findings.caveats: Panel wording is 'association', not causation. Mostly North America and Europe (83%); no scooter-specific evidence; exposure indicators NO2, EC, PM2.5 are proxies for the TRAP mixture. Several confidence intervals include 1 (childhood asthma onset NO2 1.05 (0.99-1.12); lung cancer mortality PM2.5 1.06 (0.99-1.13)), so 'moderate to high' for asthma onset in children rests on the wider body of evidence. Do not claim stroke, COPD, preterm birth or adult ALRI. The report is about TRAP in general, not a red-light queue.
findings.useOnSite: An independent expert panel (HEI, 2022, 353 studies) had high confidence that long-term traffic-related air pollution is associated with higher all-cause, circulatory and heart-disease death rates, moderate-to-high confidence for lung cancer death, new asthma in children and adults, and chest infections in young children. Individual risks per increment are modest, but very many people are exposed.

findings.verifierNote: Every number checked against the Executive Summary Table: NO2 per 10 ug/m3 all-cause 1.04 (1.01-1.06) N=11; circulatory 1.04 (1.00-1.09); IHD mortality 1.05 (1.03-1.08); lung cancer 1.04 (1.01-1.07); respiratory 1.05 (1.00-1.09); ALRI children 1.09 (1.03-1.16); asthma onset children 1.05 (0.99-1.12); adults 1.10 (1.01-1.21); diabetes prevalence 1.09 (1.02-1.17). PM2.5 per 5 ug/m3: term LBW 1.11 (1.03-1.20); SGA 1.09 (1.04-1.14); all-cause 1.03 (1.01-1.05). Additional verified PM2.5 per 5 ug/m3 values: IHD mortality 1.07 (1.04-1.10); circulatory 1.04 (1.01-1.08); stroke mortality 1.04 (1.01-1.07, rated low to moderate). Mortality estimates range 1.01-1.07 per the report; non-mortality estimates reach 1.09-1.11.
findings.claim: Meta-analytic relative risks are modest and several CIs include 1; quote increment and interval.
findings.value: NO2 per 10: all-cause 1.04 (1.01-1.06); IHD mortality 1.05 (1.03-1.08); lung cancer mortality 1.04 (1.01-1.07); ALRI children 1.09 (1.03-1.16); adult asthma onset 1.10 (1.01-1.21); childhood asthma onset 1.05 (0.99-1.12). PM2.5 per 5: IHD mortality 1.07 (1.04-1.10); all-cause 1.03 (1.01-1.05); lung cancer mortality 1.06 (0.99-1.13).
findings.citation: HEI Special Report 23 (2022), Executive Summary Table, p.9.
findings.quote: The summary estimates showed that NO2, EC, and PM2.5 were associated with all-cause, circulatory, IHD, respiratory, and lung cancer mortality, ranging from 1.01 to 1.07.
findings.caveats: Per standard increment of a proxy pollutant, not per scooter, red light or metre from a road; population averages, not individual predictions. N is the number of studies per estimate (often 3-12).
findings.useOnSite: About 4-5% higher risk of dying from heart disease or lung cancer for each 10 ug/m3 of NO2 (HEI 2022).

findings.verifierNote: The WHO publication page (ISBN 9789240034228, 290 pages) opened and confirmed the title and ISBN, but the PDF, NCBI Bookshelf table and WHO feature story could not be fetched (DSpace shell, reCAPTCHA, host not allowed), and web search budget was exhausted. No guideline value was seen in a primary source by me. Values stay as the researcher gave them and must be checked against the WHO table before printing.
findings.claim: WHO 2021 guidelines: PM2.5 5 ug/m3 annual, 15 ug/m3 24-h; PM10 15 annual, 45 24-h; NO2 10 annual, 25 24-h (2005 values: PM2.5 10 annual; NO2 40 annual).
findings.value: Values unconfirmed by me. Remaining WHO values (ozone, SO2, CO, NO2 1-hour) not retrieved.
findings.citation: World Health Organization. 2021. WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Geneva: WHO. ISBN 978-92-4-003422-8 (ISBN and title verified on WHO publication page).
findings.quote: n/a
findings.caveats: Guideline levels are health-based targets, not legal limits; Taiwan's own standards differ. Do not print numbers until verified.
findings.useOnSite: WHO's 2021 guideline is an annual average of 5 ug/m3 for PM2.5 and 10 ug/m3 for NO2 (verify before printing).

findings.verifierNote: I opened the WHO fact sheet (dated 24 Oct 2024 on the page) and saw: 'Ambient (outdoor) air pollution is estimated to have caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019'; 6.7 million for ambient plus household combined; 89% in low- and middle-income countries, greatest number in South-East Asia and Western Pacific Regions; 99% of the world lived where guidelines were not met; 68% of ambient deaths from the page text seen. The 14/14/4% splits for COPD, ALRI and lung cancer were not individually re-checked.
findings.claim: WHO estimates ambient air pollution caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019.
findings.value: 4.2 million (2019); 6.7 million ambient + household; 89% low- and middle-income countries; 99% of population above guideline levels.
findings.citation: WHO. Ambient (outdoor) air pollution. Fact sheet, 24 October 2024.
findings.quote: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution is estimated to have caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019.
findings.caveats: All sources, not traffic or scooters; modelled attribution; global; the fact sheet says the mortality is due to exposure to fine particulate matter. Do not confuse with 6.7 million.
findings.useOnSite: WHO estimates that outdoor air pollution caused about 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019.

findings.verifierNote: I opened IARC press release 221 (17 Oct 2013): outdoor air pollution Group 1, particulate matter evaluated separately also Group 1, sufficient evidence for lung cancer, positive association with bladder cancer, 223,000 lung cancer deaths in 2010, more than 1000 papers from five continents. Crossref confirms Lancet Oncol 14(13):1262-1263, 2013, Loomis et al. Volume publication year 2016 and working-group meeting dates were not seen in a source I opened.
findings.claim: IARC classified outdoor air pollution and particulate matter in it as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1), Monograph Volume 109, announced 17 October 2013.
findings.value: Group 1 both; 223,000 lung cancer deaths worldwide in 2010 attributed.
findings.citation: IARC press release No. 221, 17 October 2013. Loomis D, Grosse Y, Lauby-Secretan B, et al. 2013. The carcinogenicity of outdoor air pollution. Lancet Oncol 14(13):1262-1263. IARC Monographs Volume 109 (2016 per researcher; unverified).
findings.quote: IARC ... has classified outdoor air pollution as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1).
findings.caveats: Hazard classification, not a risk size; whole outdoor mixture, not scooter exhaust; lung cancer is the cause established, bladder only positive association.
findings.useOnSite: IARC (WHO's cancer agency) classified outdoor air pollution, and the particles in it, as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) in 2013.

findings.verifierNote: Upgraded to VERIFIED for the classification: IARC press release 213 (12 June 2012, opened) says diesel engine exhaust Group 1 (previously 2A in 1988) and 'gasoline exhaust was possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), a finding unchanged from the previous evaluation in 1989'. Correction: the press release dates the earlier diesel 2A evaluation to 1988 (monograph published 1989), not simply 1989. Publication year of Volume 105: PubMed/Europe PMC (PMID 26442290, NCBI Bookshelf NBK294269) index it as 2014; the researcher's conflict (2013 vs 2014) is resolved to 2014 for the volume, with the meeting held 5-12 June 2012 (press release 12 June 2012 after 'a week-long meeting'). Lancet Oncol 13(7):663-664 (2012) confirmed by Crossref.
findings.claim: IARC Volume 105 classified diesel engine exhaust as Group 1 and gasoline engine exhaust as Group 2B.
findings.value: Diesel Group 1; gasoline Group 2B (unchanged from 1989).
findings.citation: Benbrahim-Tallaa L, Baan RA, Grosse Y, et al. 2012. Lancet Oncol 13(7):663-664. IARC Monographs Vol 105, Diesel and Gasoline Engine Exhausts and Some Nitroarenes, IARC, Lyon, 2014 (PubMed year).
findings.quote: The Working Group concluded that gasoline exhaust was possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), a finding unchanged from the previous evaluation in 1989.
findings.caveats: A scooter is a gasoline engine: do not say IARC lists scooter exhaust as Group 1. Two-stroke scooters not separately evaluated as far as seen.
findings.useOnSite: IARC lists diesel exhaust as carcinogenic to humans and gasoline exhaust as possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B); outdoor air pollution as a whole and several exhaust components such as benzene are Group 1.

findings.verifierNote: IARC publication page for Volume 120 opened: 'Benzene, Volume 120 IARC 2018', ISBNs match, says it updates Volume 100F. The page text I extracted does not state the Group 1 classification, and I did not open Volume 100F or the Lancet Oncology summary text. Group 1 status therefore stays SECONDARY here (it is long-established, but not seen by me in a source this session). Meeting dates not verified.
findings.claim: Benzene is IARC Group 1.
findings.value: Group 1 (unverified here); Vol 120, IARC 2018.
findings.citation: IARC. 2018. Benzene. IARC Monographs Vol 120. Lyon. Summary: Loomis D, Guyton KZ, Grosse Y, et al. 2017. Lancet Oncol 18(12):1574-1575 (Crossref confirmed).
findings.quote: This volume presents an evaluation of the carcinogenicity of benzene, updating with new data the most recent evaluation provided in Volume 100F of the IARC Monographs.
findings.caveats: Occupational, high-dose evidence (mainly leukaemia); no pedestrian dose estimate.
findings.useOnSite: Benzene in petrol and exhaust is classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) once the classification is verified; this does not mean a pedestrian at a red light receives a causal dose.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened via Europe PMC; all numbers match (6282 (5716-6847); IHD 2244; stroke 2140; lung cancer 1252; COPD 645; PAF 18.6% (16.9-20.3); 8.7% Hualien to 21.8% Yunlin; New Taipei 874, Kaohsiung 829). Abstract says 'Hualian'.
findings.claim: PM2.5 accounted for about 6,282 deaths in Taiwan in 2014, 18.6% of deaths from four causes.
findings.citation: Lo WC, Shie RH, Chan CC, Lin HH. 2017. J Formos Med Assoc 116(1):32-40.
findings.quote: In 2014, PM2.5 accounted for 6282 deaths [95% confidence interval (CI), 5716-6847]
findings.caveats: Modelled attribution, all PM2.5 sources, 2014 (concentrations higher than now), not traffic or scooter specific.
findings.useOnSite: One Taiwanese study estimated that fine particles contributed to about 6,300 deaths from four causes in 2014, about one in five of those deaths (all sources, modelled).

findings.verifierNote: Opened Europe PMC abstract and PMC7614604 full text. Confirmed: Crossref authors (Hill, Lim, Weeden, Lee, Augustine, Chen, Kuan, Marongiu, ... Swanton group); Nature 616:159-167; 32,957 EGFR-driven cases in four within-country cohorts; 295 individuals, EGFR 18%, KRAS 53%; Taiwan IQR 24.3-38.2. Corrections: (1) Printed relative rates per 1 ug/m3 are 0.63 (P=0.0028) England, 0.71 (P=0.0091) South Korea, 1.82 (P=4.01e-6) Taiwan, defined as 'relative rates of EGFR-driven lung cancer incidence (per 100,000 population)'; values below 1 for two countries with a 'significant' positive relationship indicate these are not ordinary risk ratios (likely regression slopes of incidence per 100,000), so none should be quoted as a risk ratio or compared across countries. (2) Taiwan data came from 12 regions but only nine counties met the criteria (>=10 EGFR-tested cases per year, >5% of population) and were retained; cases come from the Chang Gung hospital system (n=4,599, 2011-2017), not a national registry. (3) The paper states migration could not be accounted for; the Canadian individual-level analysis found higher EGFR frequency after 3 years of high exposure (73% vs 40%, P=0.03) but not after 20 years (50% vs 38%, P=0.35).
findings.claim: Hill et al. (Nature 2023) report an area-level association between PM2.5 and EGFR-driven lung cancer incidence in England, South Korea and Taiwan, plus mouse and human-tissue evidence that PM2.5 promotes tumours in cells that already carry EGFR mutations. Mechanistic and ecological; not a Taiwanese traffic or scooter finding.
findings.value: Taiwan 'relative rate' per 1 ug/m3 1.82 (P=4.01e-6) as printed; England 0.63, South Korea 0.71 as printed; units ambiguous (see note). 32,957 cases; 295 individuals: EGFR 18%, KRAS 53% of healthy lung samples.
findings.citation: Hill W, Lim EL, Weeden CE, Lee C, Augustine M, Chen K, Kuan F-C, Marongiu F, Evans EJ Jr, Moore DA, Rodrigues FS, Pich O, et al. 2023. Lung adenocarcinoma promotion by air pollutants. Nature 616:159-167.
findings.quote: we found a significant association between PM2.5 levels and the incidence of lung cancer for 32,957 EGFR-driven lung cancer cases in four within-country cohorts.
findings.caveats: Ecological, area-level; hospital-based Taiwan data; cannot control migration or smoking; mouse work uses air pollutants generally, not scooter exhaust; proposes promotion of cells with existing mutations, not that PM2.5 causes EGFR mutations. Do not quote the 1.82 figure.
findings.useOnSite: A 2023 Nature study that included Taiwanese data suggests fine particles may promote lung cancer in lung cells that already carry a common mutation (EGFR). It is a hypothesis supported by animal and population data, not specific to scooters.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened. 57,257 participants; 1,059 lung cancer, 857 LUAD; final 648 LUAD and 6,480 controls; PGS000070 OR 2.796 (2.236-3.497); interaction not significant; quote present. Crossref: BMJ Open Respir Res 12:e002899, published Oct 2025. Abstract also notes the PRS-air pollution association was more pronounced in smokers for PGS000070.
findings.claim: Taiwanese hospital case-control: LUAD patients had higher polygenic risk scores and greater PM exposure, but no statistical interaction.
findings.value: 648 LUAD cases and 6,480 controls; PGS000070 OR 2.796 (2.236-3.497).
findings.citation: Chang SL, Chuan PM, Lai CH, Yang HW, Chen YM, Hsu HS, Chen IC. 2025. BMJ Open Respir Res 12:e002899.
findings.quote: The accumulation of air pollution did not show a gradual increase in LUAD risk.
findings.caveats: Partly null; no PM effect size in abstract.
findings.useOnSite: Do not cite as support for a dose-response.

findings.verifierNote: Opened abstract (Europe PMC) and PubMed: 384,130 adults, 842,394 records, follow-up to 31 May 2019; HRs 1.02 (0.98-1.07) and 1.15 (1.10-1.20); exercise HR 0.84 and 0.65; interaction 1.03 (1.01-1.06). Journal listed by Crossref as Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ).
findings.claim: MJ cohort: highest PM2.5 group had 15% higher natural-cause mortality than lowest.
findings.value: High vs low HR 1.15 (1.10-1.20); moderate vs low 1.02 (0.98-1.07).
findings.citation: Guo C, Yu T, Chang LY, Lin C, Yang HT, Bo Y, Zeng Y, Tam T, Lau AKH, Lao XQ. 2021. CMAJ 193:E1240-E1249.
findings.quote: a higher PM2.5 exposure was associated with a higher risk of death from natural causes compared with lower exposure (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.98-1.07, and HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.10-1.20, for the moderate and high PM2.5 exposure groups, respectively)
findings.caveats: Cut-points not in abstract; self-selected health-check population; regional PM2.5. Exercise lowered risk in every PM2.5 stratum.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese adults in the highest PM2.5 group had 15% higher risk of natural-cause death; exercise still lowered risk at every pollution level.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; HRs 1.11 (1.02-1.22), 1.15 (1.05-1.26), per-increment 1.06 (1.02-1.10), 100,629 adults, 4,046 cases, 6.24 per 1,000 person-years all match. The unit symbols are rendered '[Formula]' in both Europe PMC and the abstract, so the increment (and the eGFR threshold) remain unverified; do not state '10 ug/m3' until checked. Author list corrected: Crossref lists ... Chang LY, Hoek G, Lau AKH (not 'Ng E'); full list not captured.
findings.claim: Higher long-term PM2.5 associated with incident CKD in the MJ cohort.
findings.value: Q4 vs Q1 HR 1.11 (1.02-1.22); Q5 vs Q1 1.15 (1.05-1.26); per increment (unit unverified) 1.06 (1.02-1.10).
findings.citation: Chan TC, Zhang Z, Lin BC, Lin C, Deng HB, Chuang YC, Chan JWM, Jiang WK, Tam T, Chang LY, Hoek G, Lau AKH, et al. 2018. Environ Health Perspect 126:107002.
findings.quote: Every [increment] in the PM2.5 concentration was associated with a 6% higher risk of developing CKD (HR: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.02, 1.10). [abstract renders the unit as '[Formula]']
findings.caveats: eGFR-defined CKD on health-check data; unit missing from abstract; outside HEI list.
findings.useOnSite: Mention only as one Taiwanese cohort association, with increment confirmed from full paper.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; quartile HRs 1.28 (1.18-1.39), 1.27 (1.17-1.38), 1.16 (1.07-1.26) and 147,908 participants confirmed. Citation corrected: Crossref lists more authors than the researcher gave (after Lau AKH come further authors, final entries Lin, Chan). Abstract is also explicit that the 2-year average at 1x1 km was used.
findings.claim: MJ cohort: higher PM2.5 quartiles had 16-28% higher incident type 2 diabetes; non-monotonic.
findings.citation: Lao XQ, Guo C, Chang LY, Bo Y, Zhang Z, Chuang YC, Jiang WK, Lin C, Tam T, Lau AKH, et al. 2019. Diabetologia 62:759-769.
findings.quote: participants exposed to the second, third and fourth quartiles of ambient PM2.5 had HRs of 1.28 (95% CI 1.18, 1.39), 1.27 (95% CI 1.17, 1.38) and 1.16 (95% CI 1.07, 1.26), respectively, for the incidence of type 2 diabetes
findings.caveats: No monotonic dose-response; fasting glucose at health checks; HEI rated diabetes moderate.
findings.useOnSite: Say 'higher PM2.5 was associated with more new type 2 diabetes in Taiwanese adults' without a headline percentage.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; aHR 1.32 (1.12-1.56) incidence, 1.28 (1.01-1.63) death per 10 ug/m3, 736 cases, 401 deaths, median 12.3 y, MJ linked to Taiwan Cancer Registry; all match; quote verbatim. Note the abstract gives the mortality CI lower bound as 1.01, close to the null.
findings.claim: MJ cohort: PM2.5 associated with lung cancer incidence and mortality in never-smokers but not ever-smokers.
findings.value: Never-smokers per 10 ug/m3: incidence aHR 1.32 (1.12-1.56); death aHR 1.28 (1.01-1.63).
findings.citation: Huang HL, Chuang YH, Lin TH, Lin C, Chen YH, Hung JY, Chan TC. 2021. Int J Environ Res Public Health 18:12400.
findings.quote: For never smokers, the risk of developing LC (aHR: 1.32, 95%CI: 1.12-1.56) and dying from LC-related causes (aHR: 1.28, 95%CI: 1.01-1.63) rises significantly with every 10 μg/m3 increment of PM2.5 exposure, but not for ever smokers.
findings.caveats: Self-selected cohort; residual confounding (cooking fumes, radon, second-hand smoke); not traffic-specific; no effect in ever-smokers does not show safety.
findings.useOnSite: In a Taiwanese cohort, each 10 ug/m3 higher long-term PM2.5 was associated with about 32% higher lung cancer incidence among never-smokers (observational, one cohort).

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; 24,544 participants aged 6-24, 33,506 observations, 2000-2014; FVC -2.22% (-2.60,-1.85), FEV1 -2.94 (-3.36,-2.51), MMEF -2.79% (-3.15,-2.41); abstract states 'a 20% increase in the prevalence of poor lung function (OR 1.20; 95% CI 1.12, 1.29)'.
findings.claim: Higher 2-year PM2.5 associated with lower lung function in Taiwanese young people.
findings.value: Per 10 ug/m3: FVC -2.22%; FEV1 -2.94%; MMEF -2.79%; poor lung function OR 1.20 (1.12-1.29).
findings.citation: Guo C, Hoek G, Chang LY, Bo Y, Lin C, Huang B, Chan TC, Tam T, Lau AKH, Lao XQ. 2019. Environ Health Perspect 127:127008.
findings.quote: Every 10-μg/m3 increase in the 2-y average PM2.5 concentration was associated with decreases of 2.22% [95% confidence interval (CI): -2.60, -1.85], 2.94 (95% CI: -3.36, -2.51), and 2.79% (95% CI: -3.15, -2.41) in the FVC, FEV1, and MMEF, respectively.
findings.caveats: Regional PM2.5, not roadside; screening population; modest percent differences are not a diagnosis.
findings.useOnSite: A Taiwanese study of about 24,500 young people found higher long-term PM2.5 was associated with lower lung function (regional air, not roadside).

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; N=32,672, 2001, ORs O3 1.138 (1.001-1.293), CO 1.045 (1.017-1.074), NOx 1.005 (0.954-1.117) as printed, SO2 0.874 (0.729-1.054), PM10 0.934 (0.909-0.960) all match. Note the NOx CI is asymmetric about its point estimate as printed in the abstract; quote only with the null interval. Only the first author (Hwang) was visible in Crossref; remaining authors as given by researcher are not independently verified here.
findings.claim: Taiwanese school-children cross-sectional study: asthma associated with O3 and CO, not NOx or PM10.
findings.citation: Hwang BF, Lee YL, Lin YC, Jaakkola JJK, Guo YL. 2005. Thorax 60:467-473.
findings.quote: The results are consistent with the hypothesis that long term exposure to traffic related outdoor air pollutants such as NOx, CO, and O3 increases the risk of asthma in children.
findings.caveats: Cross-sectional, 2001 data, regional monitors; NOx null; PM10 inverse; fleet then differed.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use as a headline.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened; N=29,547, 1,720 dementia cases, 2000-2010; NO2 Q2 1.10 (0.96-1.26), Q3 1.01 (0.87-1.17), Q4 1.54 (1.34-1.77); CO Q2 1.07 (0.92-1.25), Q3 1.37 (1.19-1.58), Q4 1.61 (1.39-1.85). Note: the abstract does not describe the cohort as 'exposed quartile of nearest monitor'; that detail was not verified.
findings.claim: NHIRD cohort: highest quartile of NO2 or CO had higher dementia risk.
findings.citation: Chang KH, Chang MY, Muo CH, Wu TN, Chen CY, Kao CH. 2014. PLoS ONE 9:e103078.
findings.quote: exposure to NO2 and CO is associated with an increased risk of dementia in the Taiwanese population.
findings.caveats: Non-monotonic; claims-based diagnosis; HEI did not rate dementia.
findings.useOnSite: At most: some studies link traffic-related gases to dementia but evidence is developing.

findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened: 34,088 adults initiating dialysis, aHR 1.11 (1.08-1.13) per 10 ug/m3; quintile IV 1.09 (1.03-1.16), V 1.11 (1.05-1.19) (vs I; mean PM2.5 over 29.33 ug/m3 for levels III-V); spline lowest at 26 ug/m3, steep rise above 37.
findings.claim: Dialysis patients: 11% higher mortality per 10 ug/m3 PM2.5.
findings.citation: Chen SF, Chien YH, Chen PC. 2023. Environ Pollut 316:120606.
findings.quote: The adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) per 10-μg/m3 increase of PM2.5 for mortality was 1.11 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.08-1.13).
findings.caveats: Vulnerable subgroup; zip-code exposure; non-linear.
findings.useOnSite: Optional vulnerable-group example only.

findings.verifierNote: Opened the PubMed abstract (eutils): 2,120 children in three cohorts (1994-1998, 1997-2001, 2007-2011), mean age 11 to 15; NO2 P<0.001; PM2.5 P=0.008 FEV1, P<0.001 FVC; PM10 P<0.001; low FEV1 at 15 years 7.9% to 6.3% to 3.6% (P=0.001); boys and girls, with and without asthma. Authors/volume/pages confirmed by Crossref.
findings.claim: Southern California children: lung-function growth improved as NO2 and PM fell.
findings.citation: Gauderman WJ, Urman R, Avol E, Berhane K, McConnell R, Rappaport E, Chang R, Lurmann F, Gilliland F. 2015. N Engl J Med 372:905-913.
findings.quote: The proportions of children with clinically low FEV1 (defined as <80% of the predicted value) at 15 years of age declined significantly, from 7.9% to 6.3% to 3.6% across the three periods, as the air quality improved (P = 0.001).
findings.caveats: US, car-dominated; separate cohorts; community-level exposure; cannot rule out other secular changes.
findings.useOnSite: US children who grew up as air quality improved had better lung growth; evidence from California, not Taiwan or scooters.

findings.verifierNote: New. PubMed abstract opened (PMID 39987015). Modelled health-impact (WHO methodology) estimating post-neonatal infant deaths attributable to PM2.5 for 2006, 2015, 2023; this is a Taiwanese 'what the fall in PM2.5 was worth' estimate, not an observed accountability study. The abstract's wording on the percentages ('14.8% in 2006 to 10.3% in 2023' and '5.58-9.31% decline') is ambiguous; read the full paper before quoting any number.
findings.claim: A modelled Taiwanese estimate suggests the fall in ambient PM2.5 between 2006 and 2023 lowered the PM2.5-attributable burden of post-neonatal infant deaths.
findings.value: Attributable fraction fell from 14.8% (2006) to 10.3% (2023) per abstract; PM2.5 to 10 ug/m3 scenario 5.58-9.31% decline (interpretation unclear).
findings.citation: Chen CC, Tsai SS, Yeh CN, Yang CY. 2025. Health benefits of a reduction in ambient fine particulate matter levels for post-neonatal infant survival in Taiwan. J Toxicol Environ Health A 88(13):536-545.
findings.quote: PM2.5 concentrations fell markedly throughout Taiwan over the 20-year study period.
findings.caveats: Modelled attribution, all PM2.5 sources, not traffic or scooters; ecological; reduction not shown to be caused by any policy.
findings.useOnSite: Optional: modelled estimate that Taiwan's PM2.5 decline lowered the attributable infant burden.

doNotClaim: Do not say IARC classifies scooter or gasoline exhaust as Group 1: gasoline engine exhaust is Group 2B; diesel exhaust, outdoor air pollution, particulate matter and benzene (once verified) are Group 1.

Do not say that standing by an idling scooter pack at a red light causes cancer, asthma or heart disease, or attribute a number of Taiwanese deaths to scooters; none of the sources verified measures a pedestrian's long-term risk from queueing scooters.
Do not present the 6,282 PM2.5 deaths in 2014 (Lo 2017) as scooter deaths, as current, or as counted deaths.
Do not call HEI findings proof of causation; HEI speaks of confidence in an association, with relative risks mostly 1.03-1.10.
Do not claim HEI high confidence for stroke (low to moderate), COPD (low), preterm birth (low), adult ALRI (very low to low) or dementia (not rated).
Do not use WHO's 4.2 million for traffic or scooters, and do not confuse it with 6.7 million (ambient plus household).

Do not quote Hill et al. 2023 'relative rates' (1.82 Taiwan, 0.63 England, 0.71 Korea) as risk ratios; do not say PM2.5 causes EGFR mutations or that the study proved scooter exhaust causes lung cancer.
Do not tell people to avoid walking or exercise on the strength of the MJ cohort; exercise lowered risk in every PM2.5 stratum.
Do not state any avoided-death or monetised figure for scooter electrification in Taiwan; none was found.
Do not print WHO 2021 guideline numbers until checked against WHO's table.
Do not state the CKD per-increment unit (Chan 2018) until checked in the full paper.
